add-a-starvation-guard-to-a-github-actio.text:
← Actions runner starvation check

Add a starvation guard step to a GitHub Actions workflow

The page-and-paste tool and the check.py CLI both answer this for one run you already have the JSON for. This page is the other case: wiring the same check into your own repository so a starved run tells you so on its own, in its job summary, instead of showing up as one more red check to chase.

Why a separate workflow, not a step in the job that might starve

A job that never gets a runner never executes a single step of its own — there is nothing inside it to add a check to. And a job that did run cannot see its siblings' final status while the run is still in progress. The fix used here is a second workflow, triggered by workflow_run, that starts only after the run it is watching has completely finished. By then every sibling job — starved or not — has a final conclusion the Actions API can report.

The workflow

This version needs no external fetch at all — it asks the Actions API directly with the gh CLI that every ubuntu-latest runner already has installed, and classifies with gh api's own --jq filter:

name: starvation-guard
on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: ["*"]        # or name the specific workflow(s) to guard
    types: [completed]

jobs:
  guard:
    if: github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'failure'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: read
    steps:
      - name: Classify the run
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          gh api "repos/${{ github.repository }}/actions/runs/${{ github.event.workflow_run.id }}/jobs" \
            --jq '[.jobs[] | select(.conclusion == "failure")] |
              if length == 0 then "No failed jobs in this run."
              else .[] | if .runner_id == 0
                then "STARVED  \(.name) — no runner was ever assigned, not a real failure"
                else "REAL     \(.name) — ran on runner \(.runner_id), worth debugging"
                end
              end' | tee -a "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

This is the same field the browser tool and the check.py CLI decide on — runner_id: 0 means no runner was ever assigned. Prefer check.py itself over reimplementing the filter above if your own repository can vendor it: it also separates a still-pending job from a starved one and carries the test suite that keeps the classification correct.

Reading the result

The job summary lists one line per failed job in the run: STARVED for a job whose runner_id came back 0 — not your code, nothing to debug — and REAL for one that actually ran and is worth triaging normally. The guard step above always exits success so it never becomes one more red check for a starved run to hide behind; add | grep -q STARVED && exit 1 after the pipe instead if you want the guard job itself to fail loudly the moment it finds a starved job.

What this does not need

No fine-grained personal access token, no organization setting, and no change to the workflow being guarded. The default GITHUB_TOKEN the guard job requests with permissions: actions: read is enough — the gh CLI already on the runner picks it up from the GH_TOKEN environment variable automatically, which is the same route check.py's own credential resolution prefers.

Common questions

Why a separate workflow instead of a step inside the one that might be starved?

A job cannot reliably read its own sibling jobs' final status while they are still running, and a starved job never runs a step of its own at all -- there is nothing inside it to add a step to. A workflow_run job fires after the whole run finishes, so every sibling job (starved or not) already has a final conclusion the Actions API can report.

Does the default GITHUB_TOKEN have enough access to read job data?

It needs the actions: read permission on the triggered job. Repositories with restrictive default token permissions will not grant that automatically, so the example workflow below requests it explicitly with a permissions: block rather than relying on the account-wide default.

What does the guard job actually do with the verdict?

It writes one line per failed job into the run's job summary (GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY): STARVED for a job whose runner_id came back 0, REAL for one that actually ran. The step as written always exits success, so a starved run does not itself show up as one more red check to triage -- add a grep on STARVED afterward if you want the guard job to fail loudly instead.

index.html.text:
ACTIONS RUNNER STARVATION CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is your red GitHub Actions check even real?

A job GitHub never assigns a runner to fails in a few seconds with an empty output — indistinguishable at a glance from a real, fast failure. Paste the run's own JSON below and this page reads the one field that actually decides: runner_id. Zero means no runner was ever scheduled, so no step ever ran — the failure is not your code.

Nothing is uploaded. The JSON you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device.

1. Get the run's job JSON

Run this for the failing run (needs the gh CLI, already logged in):

gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/actions/runs/RUN_ID/jobs

No gh CLI? Open https://api.github.com/repos/OWNER/REPO/actions/runs/RUN_ID/jobs in a browser tab authenticated with a token that has Actions: read, and copy the response body.

2. Paste it here

Paste the JSON from step 1 and click Check.

Verdict

Prefer a CLI, or want this in a workflow step?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py --run RUN_ID          # exits 1 if any job was starved
python3 check.py --run RUN_ID --json   # machine-readable
python3 check.py --from-json jobs.json # classify a payload you already have, no API call

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install. It talks to the API itself via the gh CLI or a GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN it finds in your environment, which is the route a hosted CI step or an agent session actually has.

Common questions

Why did my check fail in 3 seconds with no output?

That is the signature of a job GitHub never assigned a runner to — included minutes spent, a spending limit, a payment problem, or Actions disabled on the account. Every check fails within a few seconds with an empty body, and it looks identical to a real fast failure from the checks list alone.

Why not just go by how fast it failed?

Because a real job can fail in three seconds too — a syntax error or a failing assertion on the first test does not need a runner-minute to fail. Duration looks the same either way; only runner_id tells them apart, which is the one field this tool decides on.

Does this tell me why my account stopped getting runners?

No — only whether a runner was assigned. GitHub's own run-timing endpoint reports zero billable time for private repos regardless of what ran, so it cannot attribute cost either. That answer is on your GitHub billing page; this tool only tells you whether the next few minutes are worth spending on your code or on your Actions usage.

Why do I have to paste JSON instead of it just checking for me?

Checking for you would mean either a server that sees every token pasted into it, or this page fetching on your behalf with a token it would have to hold. Neither is worth the convenience next to pasting the response you already fetched yourself with your own credentials.

More: why a GitHub Actions check goes red in seconds with no output, add a starvation guard step to your own workflow so a starved run reports itself, or this checker vs. just re-running the job.

Related: if the job did get a runner and tests flip between runs, the flaky test finder classifies which tests are flaky versus broken from JUnit XML you paste — nothing uploaded.

Related: if the job did get a runner and line coverage fell on the PR, the coverage drop check compares two Cobertura or JaCoCo reports and names the files that got worse — nothing uploaded.

vs-rerunning-the-job.html.text:
← Actions Runner Starvation Check

This checker vs. just re-running the job

Re-running the failed job is most people's first move on a red check, and it is a reasonable one -- if the job actually ran and hit a genuinely flaky test, a re-run can pass and confirm that. What it costs is a full run's worth of time, and during a starvation window it is often uninformative: a job that never got a runner the first time has no more claim on one the second time, so the same push can burn several retries before the pattern -- runner_id: 0 every single time -- becomes obvious.

This tool answers from the JSON the very first failed run already produced, before you spend a second run finding out. It reads the one field the checks tab never shows you and tells you in one click whether a runner was ever assigned.

QuestionWhere to answer it
The job ran and I suspect a flaky test -- will it pass if I try again? Re-run the job -- that is a real question about test flakiness this tool does not answer.
Did this job even get a runner the first time? This checker -- reads runner_id from the JSON you already have, no second run needed.
Six checks went red in three seconds on a change that couldn't break them all. This checker -- that pattern is the starvation signature; paste the JSON and confirm it instantly instead of guessing from how it looks.
I want this decided automatically in CI, without a person reading the checks tab. python3 check.py --run RUN_ID -- exits 1 the moment any job was starved, wireable into a workflow step.

Used together: re-run when you have a specific reason to suspect flakiness in a job that actually executed; reach for this tool first when several unrelated checks all went red at once, or before spending a retry on a job that may never get a runner anyway.

Try it

Paste the same JSON you would check before deciding to re-run anything.

Check whether it was starved

Free, runs entirely in your browser, nothing is uploaded. If the verdict is starved, actions-minutes-estimator projects which workflow is spending the allowance before the next run goes the same way.

Questions

Isn't clicking "Re-run failed jobs" the obvious first move?

It is the obvious move, and it is not wrong -- if the job actually ran and hit a flaky test, a re-run can genuinely pass and tell you something. It is just slow and, during a starvation window, uninformative: a job that never got a runner the first time has no more reason to get one the second time, so the same push can burn several retries before anyone notices the pattern is runner_id: 0 every time, not a flaky assertion.

Does re-running eventually prove whether it was starvation?

Only after the fact and only sometimes -- if a runner happens to be available on a later retry, the job passes and you never learn why it failed the first time; if runners are still starved, it fails again and looks like a flaky or broken job either way. This tool answers from the very first run's own JSON, before you spend a second run finding out.

What does this tool see that a re-run does not show me?

The run's own runner_id field, which the checks tab never surfaces. A job that was actually scheduled has a real, nonzero id; a job GitHub never got to has runner_id: 0 and an empty runner_name. That single field is proof no step could have run, and it is present on the very first failed run -- a re-run does not reveal it any better, it just spends another run's worth of time.

Is my run's JSON uploaded anywhere to get this verdict?

No. You fetch it yourself with your own gh CLI or token, paste it into this page, and the verdict is computed in your browser. Nothing about your run, your repository, or your token is sent anywhere -- the only network request in the whole flow is the one you made yourself to GitHub's API.

why-is-my-github-actions-check-red-in-se.text:
← Actions runner starvation check

Why is my GitHub Actions check red in 3 seconds with no output?

You push a commit or open a PR. Every check goes red within a handful of seconds. There is no log to open, no failing assertion, no stack trace — the output body is empty. It happens on a change that could not plausibly break six different workflows at once, including ones that touch files you never edited.

That pattern is not your code. It is the signature of a job GitHub never assigned a runner to: the account's included Actions minutes are spent, a spending limit was hit, there is a payment problem, or Actions has been disabled outright. GitHub's UI does not say any of that on the checks tab — it just shows red, the same red a real failure shows.

Why you can't tell by how fast it failed

A real job can fail in three seconds too — a syntax error, or a test suite's first assertion failing before it does anything expensive. Duration looks identical in both cases, which is exactly why it is the wrong signal to trust, in either direction: it will make you "fix" code that was never broken, and just as easily wave through a real regression because it also failed fast and got blamed on "CI being CI."

The field that actually decides

Every job GitHub Actions reports through its API carries a runner_id. A job that was actually scheduled onto a machine has a real, nonzero id. A job GitHub never got to has runner_id: 0 and an empty runner_name — proof no runner was ever assigned, which means no step in the job could have run, which means the failure cannot be about anything the job would have tested.

gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/actions/runs/RUN_ID/jobs | jq '.jobs[] | {name, runner_id, runner_name}'

If every job in that output shows "runner_id": 0, none of those checks are telling you anything about your change. If they show a real id, the failure is real and worth debugging normally.

Paste that same JSON into the Actions Runner Starvation Check page for a plain verdict instead of reading the fields by eye, or run the zero-dependency check.py CLI in a script so it can decide for you: python3 check.py --run RUN_ID exits 1 the moment any job was starved.

What this does not tell you

Only that a runner was or was not assigned — not why your account stopped getting them. GitHub's own run-timing endpoint reports zero billable milliseconds for private repositories regardless of what actually ran, so it is no help attributing the cause either. Exhausted minutes, a spending limit, a payment problem, and Actions being disabled all look identical from the Actions API; that distinction is on your GitHub billing page, not something any tool reading the jobs API can recover.

No warranty. This page and the tool it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. They are not a substitute for reading GitHub's own billing and Actions usage pages. Verify before relying on the output.
